entry.title: Continuous and discrete optimization: a working map

link.title: Continuous and discrete optimization: a working map

entry.content:
Almost every optimization problem reduces to the same three objects: variables you can choose, an objective to make small, and constraints that say which choices are allowed.

\[\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}} \; f(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{subject to} \quad g_i(\mathbf{x}) \le 0, \quad h_j(\mathbf{x}) = 0\]

What determines whether the problem takes a second or a century is the structure: whether \(\mathcal{X}\) is continuous or discrete, whether \(f\) is convex, whether you can compute derivatives, and whether the data is known or random.

The single biggest fork is continuous versus discrete, and the practical difference is larger than the notation suggests. This post is the map I wish I had been given early: what lives on each side, which methods belong where, how to diagnose which kind of problem you have, and what happens at the border: which is where most interesting applied work actually sits.

Part I · Continuous optimization

Variables are real-valued. You can take derivatives, make arbitrarily small steps, and ask what happens in a neighbourhood. The local geometry is informative, which is what makes the whole theory possible.

The dividing line: convexity

A convex problem has a convex objective over a convex feasible set. Its consequence is the most useful single fact in optimization:

Every local minimum is global, and there is a certificate that you have found it.

So “did I find the answer?” has a yes-or-no answer. For convex problems with structure we have polynomial-time algorithms, mature solvers, and duality theory that turns the question “is this optimal?” into an arithmetic check. Convex optimization is, for practical purposes, a solved technology.

Non-convex is everything else, and the honest summary is that you are looking for a good point rather than the point. What we have are methods that reliably find stationary points, plus empirical knowledge about which landscapes are forgiving. Deep learning is the famous case where non-convexity turned out to matter far less than everyone feared.

The conic hierarchy

Convex problems come in a nested family, and knowing where yours sits tells you which solver to use:

Class Objective / constraints Example
LP linear / linear production planning, network flow, diet problem
QP quadratic / linear portfolio variance, SVM dual, MPC
SOCP linear / second-order cone robust LP, facility location with distances
SDP linear / positive-semidefinite relaxations of hard combinatorial problems, control

Each contains the one above it. The interesting fact is that interior-point methods solve all of them with essentially one algorithmic idea (follow a central path toward the boundary) which is why a single solver can handle the whole hierarchy.

Unconstrained methods, and what each one buys

Everything here is a different answer to: how much do you know about the local shape?

Gradient descent, \(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k - \alpha\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)\). Uses the slope only. Cheap, and slow when the problem is badly conditioned: the convergence rate degrades with the condition number, which is why a long narrow valley makes it zig-zag.

Momentum / Nesterov acceleration, accumulate past directions. For convex problems this improves the rate from \(O(1/k)\) to \(O(1/k^2)\), and that is provably the best a first-order method can do. Acceleration is not a trick; it is a matching upper bound.

Newton’s method, \(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{H}^{-1}\nabla f\). Uses curvature. Quadratic local convergence; condition number stops mattering because you are rescaling by the geometry itself. Costs \(O(d^3)\) per step, and on a non-convex problem \(\mathbf{H}\) can be indefinite, in which case the “descent” direction goes uphill.

Quasi-Newton (BFGS, L-BFGS), build a curvature estimate from successive gradients via the secant equation. The practical sweet spot for medium-scale smooth problems, and L-BFGS’s limited memory makes it workable at high dimension. Its weakness: the estimate is built from gradient differences, so with stochastic gradients you are differencing noise.

Trust-region and line-search methods, two ways to answer “how far should I step?”. A line search picks the step length along a fixed direction; a trust region fixes a radius you trust the model within and optimises inside it. Trust regions are more robust on non-convex problems, because they handle indefinite curvature gracefully instead of needing a fix.

Sketched and randomized second-order methods, compute curvature on a random subspace. Sample \(m \ll d\) Hessian columns and reconstruct via the Nyström method, bringing cost from \(O(nd^2 + d^3)\) to \(O(ndm + dm^2)\). This is my own area; the design problem is getting a usable descent direction out of a low-rank approximation of a possibly indefinite matrix, which regularisation solves.

Derivative-free methods (Nelder-Mead, pattern search, CMA-ES): when there is no gradient: simulation output, a physical experiment, a black box. Slow and sometimes the only option.

Bayesian optimization: when evaluations are expensive as well as derivative-free. Build a probabilistic surrogate, use an acquisition function to choose the next point. Dozens of evaluations, not thousands.

Constrained methods

KKT conditions generalise “the gradient is zero” to constrained problems: at an optimum, the objective gradient is a combination of active constraint gradients. The multipliers are shadow prices (how much the optimum would improve if a constraint were relaxed) which is often more useful to a practitioner than the solution itself.

Lagrangian duality turns the constrained problem into an unconstrained one in the multipliers. The dual is always a lower bound; for convex problems the gap is zero. That gap is what lets you certify optimality.

The main families:

  • Interior-point, add a barrier that blows up at the boundary, shrink it. Workhorse for convex problems at scale.
  • Active-set, guess which constraints bind, solve the equality-constrained problem, repeat.
  • Augmented Lagrangian / ADMM, penalise violation and update multipliers. ADMM splits a problem into pieces that are each easy, and is the reason so much distributed and federated optimization is built on it: the splitting maps onto the machines.
  • Projected and proximal gradient, step, then project back into the feasible set. The proximal version handles non-smooth terms, which is what makes \(\ell_1\) regularisation tractable and gives you sparsity.

Stochastic optimization

When the objective is an expectation, over data, or over genuine randomness:

\[\min_{\mathbf{x}} \; \mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[F(\mathbf{x},\xi)\right]\]

SGD replaces the gradient with a cheap unbiased estimate. The variance of that estimate, not the curvature, sets the convergence rate: which is a different world from the deterministic case and calls for different methods.

Variance reduction (SVRG, SAGA, SARAH) uses a control variate, typically a periodically refreshed full gradient, to cut the noise, recovering linear convergence on strongly convex problems. My JIMO paper sits here: using Barzilai-Borwein step sizes as cheap second-order information inside SVRG, where “cheap” means the gradients were already computed.

Robust and chance-constrained optimization handle uncertainty differently, optimise the worst case over an uncertainty set, or require constraints to hold with probability \(1-\epsilon\). Often the right framing in engineering, where a constraint violation is a failure rather than a cost.

Part II · Discrete optimization

Variables take values in a finite or countable set: integers, binary choices, permutations, subsets, graph structures. Scheduling, routing, assignment, network design, and most of operations research.

Why it is categorically harder

There is no local geometry. You cannot take a derivative of a decision. You cannot take a small step, flipping one binary variable may be the only move available, and it may be a large change. A solution can be optimal among all its neighbours and far from the global optimum, with nothing local to indicate it.

And the problems are genuinely hard: TSP, knapsack, set cover, graph colouring are NP-hard, so barring a complexity surprise there is no polynomial algorithm. This is not a gap in our knowledge of algorithms; it is believed to be a property of the problems.

So the discipline changes. In continuous convex optimization you ask “what is the optimum?”. In discrete optimization you ask one of:

  • What is the best solution I can find in the time available? (heuristics)
  • How far from optimal might I be? (bounds and gaps)
  • Can I prove optimality for instances of this size? (exact methods)

Exact methods

Branch and bound is the core idea and it is beautiful in its simplicity. Relax the integrality constraint and solve the easy continuous problem. That gives a bound. If the relaxed solution happens to be integral, you are done. Otherwise pick a fractional variable and branch: one subproblem with \(x \le \lfloor v \rfloor\), one with \(x \ge \lceil v \rceil\). Recurse. Any subtree whose bound is worse than the best solution found is pruned without being explored.

The whole art is making the bound tight, because a tight bound prunes aggressively and a loose one makes you enumerate.

Cutting planes tighten the relaxation by adding valid inequalities that cut off fractional solutions without removing any integer point. Branch and cut (doing both) is what every modern MILP solver actually is, and why Gurobi and CPLEX routinely solve problems with hundreds of thousands of integer variables that are “NP-hard” in the textbook sense. The theory says worst case; the solvers exploit structure.

Dynamic programming works when the problem has optimal substructure: shortest paths, knapsack, sequence alignment. Exact and polynomial in the state space, and the state space is usually what explodes.

Constraint programming takes a different route: propagate constraints to shrink variable domains, search what remains. Often dominant on scheduling and rostering, where the constraints are complex and combinatorial rather than numerical.

SAT and SMT solvers reduce the problem to Boolean satisfiability. Modern CDCL solvers handle millions of clauses, which is one of the genuinely surprising engineering achievements in computing.

When exact is out of reach

Approximation algorithms come with a proven guarantee, within a factor of optimal, always. The greedy algorithm for set cover is within \(\ln n\); for submodular maximisation under a cardinality constraint, greedy achieves \(1 - 1/e\) and that is provably the best possible. A guarantee is worth a great deal in a setting where you otherwise have no idea how good your answer is.

Metaheuristics have no guarantee and often work well: simulated annealing (accept worse solutions with decreasing probability, borrowed from statistical physics), tabu search (forbid recent moves to escape local optima), genetic and evolutionary algorithms, ant colony optimization, large neighbourhood search. The last is the most practically effective for routing: destroy part of a solution and rebuild it optimally.

Heuristic search, A*, best-first, beam search, Monte Carlo Tree Search. Here the heuristic function is everything: a good admissible heuristic can turn an intractable search into a quick one, and the whole engineering problem becomes estimating cost-to-go well. I work on exactly this in my current role, in a combinatorial AND/OR search setting.

Part III · Where the two halves meet

Most interesting applied problems live here, and this is the part that pure-continuous or pure-discrete training leaves out.

Relaxation. Drop integrality, solve the continuous problem, and you get a bound plus a starting point. This is the engine inside branch and bound, and it is why discrete optimization depends so heavily on continuous optimization being fast.

LP relaxation and rounding. Solve the LP, round the fractional solution, prove the rounding costs you at most a factor. Randomised rounding gives some of the best known approximation guarantees.

Semidefinite relaxation. The Goemans-Williamson algorithm for MAX-CUT relaxes a binary quadratic problem to an SDP and rounds with a random hyperplane, achieving 0.878 of optimal. A continuous, convex relaxation of an NP-hard discrete problem, with a proven guarantee, one of the most elegant results in the field.

MINLP. Both continuous and discrete variables with nonlinear functions: chemical process design, unit commitment in power systems, portfolio problems with transaction lots. Genuinely hard, and exactly what industrial problems look like.

Decomposition. Benders splits a problem into a master problem over the discrete variables and subproblems over the continuous ones, iterating by passing cuts. Dantzig-Wolfe and column generation do the dual thing (generate variables on demand) and are how vehicle routing and crew scheduling are solved at airline scale.

Submodularity is the closest discrete analogue of convexity. Diminishing returns on sets gives you provable guarantees for greedy algorithms, and it shows up in sensor placement, feature selection, summarisation and data selection.

Optimal transport sits precisely on the boundary. The discrete problem is an assignment problem a linear program with integral optimal solutions by total unimodularity. The entropy-regularised continuous version is solved by Sinkhorn iterations in a few lines, which is why OT became practical in machine learning.

How to tell which problem you have

A decision procedure I actually use:

1 · Are the decisions divisible? “How much” is continuous; “which one”, “how many”, “yes or no” is discrete. Mixing both means MINLP, and you should expect difficulty.

2 · Can you compute a gradient? Analytically or by automatic differentiation, use a first- or second-order method. If not, is each evaluation cheap (derivative-free) or expensive (Bayesian optimization)?

3 · Is it convex? Check the composition rules rather than guessing: affine functions, norms, max of convex functions, and compositions respecting curvature and monotonicity. If it is convex, say so and use the right solver, you get a certificate of optimality, which is worth a lot.

4 · How large, and in what dimension? \(10^3\) variables and \(10^9\) variables are different engineering problems with the same mathematics. For discrete problems, ask instead how large the relaxation gap is, that, not the variable count, predicts whether branch and bound will finish.

5 · Is the data known? Deterministic, stochastic (optimise an expectation), or robust (optimise the worst case) are three different problems with the same description in words, and choosing the wrong one is a common and expensive mistake.

6 · What resource is actually scarce? Time, memory, communication rounds, instrument hours, money. This determines what you are really minimising, and it is the question most often skipped including in the academic literature, which tends to count iterations because iterations are easy to count.

Software worth knowing

Need Tools
LP / MILP / QP Gurobi, CPLEX, HiGHS (open), SCIP, CBC
Convex modelling CVXPY, JuMP, MOSEK
Nonlinear IPOPT, SNOPT, KNITRO, scipy.optimize
Constraint programming OR-Tools CP-SAT, Gecode
SAT / SMT MiniSat, CaDiCaL, Z3
Metaheuristics OR-Tools routing, LocalSolver
Bayesian optimization BoTorch, Optuna, Ax
Deep-learning optimizers PyTorch torch.optim, Optax
Benchmarking CUTEst, MIPLIB, TSPLIB

A practical note: CP-SAT is now extremely strong on scheduling and rostering, and is often the right first attempt for problems people reflexively model as MILP.

Why both halves are worth knowing

I was trained in continuous optimization, my thesis was second-order methods for large-scale unconstrained problems, which is about as continuous as it gets. Industrial problems have not respected the boundary once.

A real problem arrives as “schedule these experiments on this instrument within this budget”, and it contains a continuous surrogate model, a discrete selection, and a resource constraint, all at once. The continuous theory tells you how to fit the surrogate and how fast you can descend. The discrete theory tells you that selection is a search and that a good bound beats a clever heuristic. The boundary techniques (relaxation, decomposition, submodularity) are how the two get connected.

Knowing only one half means reaching for the wrong tool roughly half the time, and the failure is quiet: you get an answer, it is plausible, and you never learn it was the wrong formulation.

Related: where optimization lives in modern AI · what a Hessian sketch actually buys you · my research
entry.summary: The two halves of mathematical optimization, what separates them, which methods belong where, how to tell which kind of problem you actually have, and where the two meet.

entry.title: When every experiment has a price

link.title: When every experiment has a price

entry.content:
Bayesian optimization answers a specific question: given what you have measured so far, what should you measure next? It is the right tool when evaluations are expensive: a wet-lab experiment, training a large model, a physical measurement that occupies an instrument for an hour.

Almost all of the published benchmarking counts iterations. Twenty evaluations, fifty, a hundred; plot best-value-so-far against evaluation number; compare the curves.

That axis is wrong for most of the settings the method is sold for, and the gap is not subtle.

Iterations are not the budget

A laboratory does not have an iteration budget. It has instrument hours, reagents, technician time and bookings. A compute cluster has node-hours and a quota. And critically, different evaluations cost different amounts: a coarse scan and a fine scan are not the same purchase, and the acquisition function that proposes them does not know the difference unless you tell it.

Two consequences follow immediately, and the iteration-counting literature mostly skips both.

A policy that wins per iteration can lose per unit cost

If method A reaches a good value in 30 evaluations and method B takes 45, A wins the usual plot. But if A’s proposals are systematically expensive (it likes the settings that take an hour) and B’s are cheap, B may reach the same value for half the spend. On the axis that matches the actual constraint, B is better. On the axis in the paper, A is.

This is not hypothetical and it is not news: cost-aware acquisition has been studied since at least the expected improvement per second work in the early 2010s, and there is a steady line of follow-up on cost-aware and multi-fidelity variants. What has not really followed is the benchmarking convention. Most comparisons still count steps.

A campaign can simply fail to finish

This one I find more interesting, because it is a failure mode rather than a suboptimality.

Suppose your remaining budget is small, and the acquisition function: which knows nothing about money, proposes the most informative experiment available, which happens to be expensive. You cannot afford it. Now what?

Options are all bad. Run it anyway and overspend. Refuse it and have the loop propose the same thing again. Fall back to something arbitrary. Stop early.

So “how well did the policy do?” is not a well-formed question. The well-formed version has two parts: what did it achieve, and did the campaign complete within its budget. A policy with excellent final regret that only finishes 3 campaigns out of 29 is not a good policy. It is a policy you cannot deploy.

I have not often seen completion rate reported as a metric. It should be.

What a budget-aware loop actually needs

Making this structural rather than reported-after-the-fact takes three pieces:

A cost model. A function \(c(x)\) giving the price of evaluating at \(x\). Sometimes you can fit it from historical runs; sometimes it is known in closed form. Whether it is closed form matters more than it sounds: if it is, the set of affordable points is known exactly before you spend anything, so the constraint can be applied inside the acquisition optimization rather than checked afterwards.

A ledger. Something that tracks what has been spent, what remains, and refuses a proposal it cannot pay for. Boring, and it is the component that makes everything else honest.

A constrained acquisition step. Not “maximise expected improvement, then check the price” maximise expected improvement over the affordable set. The difference shows up exactly at the end of a campaign, where the behaviour matters most.

There is also a constraint that is easy to miss: a real instrument is often booked in slots, so there is a cap on what a single evaluation may consume, separate from the total. That is a restriction on the problem rather than a new policy, and it changes which policies win.

Does looking further ahead help?

The natural next thought is non-myopia. A greedy acquisition function optimises the next evaluation. If you can afford three more, shouldn’t you plan all three, maybe spend on something cheap and informative now to enable a better choice later?

In theory, clearly yes; the fully non-myopic problem is a dynamic program and the greedy policy is a one-step approximation to it. In practice the lookahead costs real compute, it compounds surrogate error over the horizon, and the two-step version is usually the only tractable one.

My honest expectation, before measuring, would be that two-step lookahead frequently does not pay at realistic budgets, and that when it does not, the reason is in the surrogate’s uncertainty estimates rather than in the planning. That is a testable claim and it is the kind of thing worth publishing either way: a negative result with a mechanism tells you where to look next, which a positive result on a synthetic benchmark often does not.

Why I think the framing is the contribution

None of the ingredients here is new. Cost-aware acquisition is established; non-myopic BO has a literature; ledgers are bookkeeping.

What seems genuinely underserved is the evaluation convention, reporting regret against cumulative cost rather than iteration count, and reporting completion rate as a first-class metric alongside final value. Those two changes are cheap, they do not require a new algorithm, and they change which methods look good.

I am building a public benchmark on exactly this, on open synthetic test functions with cost models defined in the open, so the comparison is reproducible on a laptop. When it is ready it will be linked from Projects.

Related reading: Snoek, Larochelle & Adams (2012) on expected improvement per second; Lam, Willcox & Wolpert on non-myopic BO; and the cost-aware BO line that follows from both.
entry.summary: Bayesian optimization is usually benchmarked in iterations. Laboratories do not run on iterations. What changes when you count cost instead.

entry.title: Nys-Fed: making second-order federated learning fit on an edge device

link.title: Nys-Fed: making second-order federated learning fit on an edge device

entry.content:
This post walks through Nys-Fed, a paper I co-authored with Sagnik Ghosh, Arnav Bhavsar, Varun Dutt and Dinesh Singh at IIT Mandi, published at IEEE IJCNN 2026 (WCCI). It is the federated chapter of the Nyström curvature line I have been working on since my PhD, and it is the clearest example I have of a theoretical idea that turns into a practical capability.

The short version: second-order federated optimization converges in far fewer communication rounds than first-order methods, and almost nobody uses it because the Hessian does not fit on a phone. Replacing the Hessian with a sampled low-rank sketch takes the per-round cost for a ResNet-18 from tens of hours to about two minutes.

1. Why federated learning is really a communication problem

In federated learning the data never leaves the client. Each device computes something from its own data (gradients, or model updates) and sends only that to a parameter server, which aggregates and sends a global model back. Nothing privacy-revealing crosses the network.

The cost that dominates is communication rounds. Every round means every participating device uploading, the server aggregating, and the result coming back down, across links that are slow, metered and unreliable, to devices that may not even be awake. So the question that matters is not “how many gradient steps?” but “how few rounds can we finish in?”

FedAvg and FedProx are first-order methods. They work, they are cheap per round, and they take a lot of rounds, and they degrade badly when client data is non-IID, which in practice it always is. Your phone’s photos do not look like mine.

2. The second-order case, and why it is usually ignored

Newton-type methods use curvature, not just slope. They point more directly at the minimum, so they need dramatically fewer rounds. On non-IID data the advantage is larger still, because curvature carries information about the local geometry that an averaged gradient throws away.

Newton-type descent against SGD-based paths of the kind used in FedAvg, FedProx and FOMO. Fewer, better-directed steps, if you can afford the curvature. Figure from the Nys-Fed paper.

The reason nobody does it is arithmetic. For a model with \(d\) parameters the Hessian is \(d \times d\). For ResNet-18, \(d \approx 11.7\) million, so the Hessian has about \(1.4 \times 10^{14}\) entries. In 32-bit floats that is over half a petabyte. You cannot form it, you cannot store it, you certainly cannot invert it, and you absolutely cannot send it anywhere.

Existing second-order federated methods work around this in sensible but limited ways. FedNew computes the Hessian once and reuses it, refreshing periodically, but a refresh costs as much as plain Newton. FedNS and FLeNS use Newton sketching with a random transform, which reduces what gets communicated but still needs the Hessian to produce the sketch. DONE approximates the local Hessian using Richardson iterations after several local steps.

All of them improve the descent direction. None of them makes the memory problem go away on a device with a few hundred megabytes of GPU.

3. The idea: never build the Hessian

Here is the move. Do not approximate the Hessian after computing it. Sample it.

Pick \(m \ll d\) column indices uniformly at random. Compute only those \(m\) columns, giving a thin matrix \(\mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times m}\), and let \(\mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be the intersection block. The Nyström method reconstructs an approximation of the full matrix from that slice:

\[\mathbf{N} = \mathbf{C}\,\mathbf{M}^{-1}\,\mathbf{C}^{\top}\]

Take the SVD of \(\mathbf{M}\) to get the best rank-\(k\) version. The full \(d \times d\) matrix is never formed at any point.

Nyström approximation of the Hessian at the client. Only sampled columns and the small intersection block are ever computed. Figure from the Nys-Fed paper.

The detail that makes it work

Written naively this breaks on neural networks. A deep model’s loss is non-convex, so its Hessian is indefinite (it has negative eigenvalues) and a direction built from an indefinite matrix is not guaranteed to point downhill at all. A low-rank approximation inherits the problem.

The fix is the \(\ell_2\) regularizer that is already in the objective. For

\[\min_{\mathbf{w}} \Big\{ f(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i(\mathbf{w}) + \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \Big\}\]

the Hessian is \(\mathbf{H} = \sum_i \nabla^2 f_i(\mathbf{w}) + \lambda\mathbf{I}\), and because the \(\lambda\) carries into the sampled blocks, \(\mathbf{M}\) becomes positive definite. The sketch is a fixed-rank Nyström approximation, the direction is a descent direction, and the smallest eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{M}^{-1}\) is controlled: which is what the convergence argument needs.

In the paper we go further: \(\rho_k\) is set to \(-\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{W}_k)\) when that quantity is negative and to \(\|\mathbf{g}_k\|\) otherwise, which keeps the approximated matrix positive definite across every deep model we tested rather than only in the convex case.

Inverting it without inverting it

The remaining cost is the inverse. Here the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity does the work: an inverse of a \(d \times d\) matrix with a rank-\(m\) structure becomes an inverse of an \(m \times m\) matrix plus some matrix-vector products. With \(m\) in the tens and \(d\) in the millions, that is the difference between impossible and routine.

Keeping the curvature private

Sending a curvature estimate is not obviously privacy-preserving. Following FedNew, Nys-Fed runs a one-pass ADMM step over the sketched Hessian, so what leaves the client is an ADMM-passed update rather than curvature itself:

\[\mathbf{y}_i^k = \big(\mathbf{N}^k_i + \alpha_k\mathbf{I} + \rho\mathbf{I}\big)^{-1}\big(\mathbf{g}_i^k - \lambda_i^{k-1} + \rho\,\mathbf{y}^{k-1}\big)\]

The server averages the \(\mathbf{y}_i^k\) across clients, updates the global weights, and each client updates its dual variable. One pass (not an inner ADMM loop) which is what keeps the client cost near first-order.

The federated setting: curvature is sketched on-device, passed through one ADMM step, and aggregated at the parameter server. Figure from the Nys-Fed paper.

Per global update this gives \(O(\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})\) communication and \(O(d\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})\) convergence time.

4. What the numbers say

Deep models: the headline

Communication time per round, under the same recommended model and hyperparameter settings:

Model DONE FedNew FedNS Nys-Fed
ResNet-18 (11.4M params) ≥ 48 h ≥ 132 h ≥ 48 h 130-141 s
ResNet-50 (23.9M params) ≥ 56 h ≥ 156 h ≥ 100 h 700-820 s
Custom DNN (0.1M params) ≥ 20 h ≥ 72 h ≥ 100 h 105-250 s

That is not a tuning win. It is a change in what is possible on the hardware, hours to minutes.

One asymmetry worth stating plainly, because it cuts against the obvious reading. For FedNew and FedNS on the deep models, parameters were frozen up to the last layer and the inverse Hessian computed only for that layer. Nys-Fed computed its sketch over all learnable parameters. So the baselines were given the easier job and still took hours. Without that note the table is not interpretable, which is exactly why it belongs here.

Convex models, like-for-like against DONE

On the phishing dataset, where both methods can run properly:

  DONE, 2 local iters Nys-Fed, 8 cols DONE, 5 iters Nys-Fed, 16 cols DONE, 10 iters Nys-Fed, 64 cols
Time per epoch (s) 151 7.6 513.5 16 745.1 45.3
Time for 1000 epochs (h) 41.6 2.11 142.6 4.4 206.9 12.58
phishing, logistic loss, semilog. Nys-Fed against first-order (FedAvg, FedAdam, FedProx) and second-order (FedNew, FedNS, DONE) baselines. Figure from the Nys-Fed paper.

Across datasets and architectures

Left: femnist on ResNet-18. Right: cinic10 on a custom residual model, federated via a Dirichlet split with α = 0.5. Figures from the Nys-Fed paper.

Evaluated on femnist and shakespeare from LEAF (the latter non-IID across 1,129 clients with a 1.1M-parameter LSTM for next-character prediction), cinic10 split by Dirichlet(0.5), and phishing / w8a / realsim from libsvm with logistic and L2-SVM objectives. Baselines span both families: FedAvg, FedProx, FedAdam on one side; FedNew, FedNS, DONE on the other.

5. What this does not show

The limits, because a results table without them is marketing.

  • Communication time, not wall-clock training time. The tables measure the per-round communication cost. They are not end-to-end training comparisons.
  • DONE ran with one Richardson iteration. DONE’s own paper reports better convergence with more local iterations; the comparison is at the setting that matches Nys-Fed’s single-local-update framework, which is the fair framework comparison but not DONE at its best.
  • \(m\) is a hyperparameter. The convex tables vary it from 8 to 64 columns deliberately, and the cost scales with it. There is no automatic choice.
  • The gains depend on \(d\) being large. That is the whole premise: the sketch avoids a cost you only pay at scale. At small \(d\) there is nothing to save.
  • Single-objective, classification and language modelling. No claim about other task families.

6. Why I like this result

Most of my PhD was convergence proofs and CUTEst benchmarks. It is satisfying work and the feedback loop is long and abstract.

This is the same mathematics: a sampled low-rank approximation of a matrix you cannot afford to build, regularized so the direction stays usable, pointed at a constraint that is completely concrete: this device has 400 MB of GPU memory and a metered connection. The mathematics does not change. What changes is that the answer is now the difference between a method that runs and a method that does not.

That is the line of work I want to keep doing: the part of optimization theory that turns into something that fits on the hardware you actually have.

Code and citation

Implementation from the paper, by my co-author Sagnik Ghosh: github.com/sagnik04g/Nys-Fed

Nys-Fed: Communication and Memory Efficient Nyström Approximated Curvature for Federated Learning. Sagnik Ghosh, Hardik Tankaria, Arnav Bhavsar, Varun Dutt, Dinesh Singh. IEEE International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN), IEEE World Congress on Computational Intelligence (WCCI), Maastricht, 2026.

Related work of mine on the same curvature line: NysReg-Gradient (IJCNN 2026) and Regularized Nyström for non-convex optimization. Background on the sketch itself: what a Hessian sketch actually buys you.
entry.summary: Newton-type methods converge in far fewer communication rounds than FedAvg, and nobody uses them, because a Hessian for a 25M-parameter model does not fit on a client. Here is what a Nyström sketch changes, with numbers.

entry.title: Pre-registering an experiment you expect to fail

link.title: Pre-registering an experiment you expect to fail

entry.content:
Most things you try do not work. This is not a complaint about research; it is the base rate. If you test ten ideas and two pay off, you are doing well.

The uncomfortable corollary is that your methodology has to be good enough to tell the two from the eight, and the default way of working is not. Not because anyone is dishonest, but because the ordinary sequence of events quietly rewards the wrong answer:

  1. Try something.
  2. Look at the numbers.
  3. Decide what the comparison was.

Step 3 is where it goes wrong. Once you have seen the data there are a dozen defensible ways to slice it, and you will (in complete good faith) pick one that happens to favour what you just built. Nobody has to cheat for this to happen. It is just what happens when the analysis is chosen after the result.

Here are four practices that, over the last couple of years, have changed how much I trust my own conclusions. None is original. All of them are cheap. I now find work that does not use them hard to read.

1. Write the design down before you run it

Before the run: what is being compared, on what data, with what metric, how many seeds, and what result would count as the method not working. Commit that to the repository. Do not edit it afterwards.

The first time I did this properly, the pre-registration said in advance that if the effect did not appear on a held-out external set, the method had not worked. The effect did not appear on the external set. Because that sentence was already written down and committed, there was no conversation about whether external validation was really the right test: the question had been settled while I still had no idea what the answer would be.

That is the whole mechanism. You are not proving your integrity to anyone. You are removing your future self’s ability to rationalise, at a moment when you are the only person who could catch it.

The strange part is how often the pre-registration improves the experiment. Writing “what would falsify this?” before running it tends to reveal that your planned comparison would not have answered the question at all.

2. Compare pairs, not percentages

“Method A scores 0.72, method B scores 0.77” is almost no information. How many items? How much do they vary? Did B win on the same items A won, or different ones?

Run both on the same items and compare the paired outcomes. For binary results, solved or unsolved, correct or incorrect, McNemar’s test asks the only question that matters: among items where the two methods disagreed, how lopsided was the disagreement? Eight wins and zero losses means something. Forty wins and thirty-two losses is the same aggregate difference and means almost nothing.

For continuous outcomes, bootstrap a confidence interval. It takes four lines and it converts “B is better” into “B is better by somewhere between this and that”, which is a claim someone can actually act on.

3. State the detection floor

This is the one I would most like to see become standard, because it is nearly free and it prevents a whole category of mistake.

A detection floor is one sentence: at this sample size and this variance, we cannot resolve a difference smaller than Δ. You compute it once, from the spread you already measured.

Why it matters: without it, a small improvement is indistinguishable from noise and the reader has no way to tell which they are looking at. With it, “+0.3% on 20 seeds, floor 0.9%” reads immediately as we found nothing: which is a real result, honestly reported, and stops you and everyone after you from building on sand.

I have seen more wasted effort come from un-floored small effects than from any other single methodological gap.

4. Report the negative results, with the mechanism

A write-up that only reports what worked is less useful than one that says: we tried five things, four lost, here is why.

This is partly about other people’s time. It is mostly about yours. The negative results are what tell you where the problem actually is. If four search-side interventions all fail and one succeeds, that pattern is a much stronger signal about the structure of the problem than the single success is.

And “it did not work” is not the finding. The mechanism is the finding. A more sophisticated method that loses to a simpler one is uninteresting until you can say what it was spending its extra capability on and why that did not pay. Then it is interesting, and it generalises.

The practice that catches what care does not

Everything above is still you, checking your own work.

The thing that has caught the most actual errors in my work is having someone else re-derive the headline numbers from the raw data, independently, without reading my analysis code. It finds the class of mistake that no amount of care prevents, because care operates inside your own assumptions.

The most common thing it finds is not an arithmetic error. It is a number that has drifted from its denominator: a figure that was correct when it was made, quoted later in a context where its population had changed, and then repeated. Both the figure and the sentence around it look fine. They just no longer refer to the same set of items.

A cheap mechanical version of this: a script that re-derives every published number from committed raw data and reads no analysis file. Run it in CI. A figure that no longer follows from its data becomes a build failure rather than something a colleague notices in a meeting six months later.

The cost

Maybe 10-15% more time per experiment. Against which: the ideas that survive this process are ones I will defend in a review, and I no longer have the background hum of wondering whether a result I reported last year was real.

For an individual researcher that is a good trade. For a team, where one wrong number propagates into everyone else’s planning, it is not close.
entry.summary: Four practices that changed how much I trust my own results, and the one that catches the error no amount of care prevents.

entry.title: What a Hessian sketch actually buys you

link.title: What a Hessian sketch actually buys you

entry.content:
Every introduction to optimization tells you the same two things. Gradient descent is cheap and slow. Newton’s method is expensive and fast. Then almost every practitioner uses the cheap one and spends the savings on hyperparameter tuning.

That is the right call more often than the textbooks imply. But it is worth understanding exactly what is expensive, because the expensive part is narrower than people assume, and once you know which term dominates, you can go after it.

The arithmetic

Suppose you are minimising a loss over \(d\) parameters using \(n\) data points.

Gradient descent needs the gradient: one pass over the data, \(O(nd)\) per step. It tells you which direction is downhill.

Newton’s method also wants the Hessian: the \(d \times d\) matrix of second derivatives, which tells you how the slope is changing. Forming it costs \(O(nd^2)\), and solving the linear system \(H \delta w = -g\) costs \(O(d^3)\).

That \(d^3\) is the problem. At \(d = 1{,}000\) it is a billion operations, annoying. At \(d = 10{,}000\) it is \(10^{12}\): a non-starter, and \(10{,}000\) parameters is a small model by any modern standard.

So the field went sideways instead. L-BFGS keeps a short history of gradient differences and builds an implicit curvature estimate from them, never forming a matrix at all. It works remarkably well, and it is still the default when someone needs a second-order method at scale.

The question worth asking

L-BFGS infers curvature from first-order information, from how the gradient has changed over the last few steps. That is clever, and it is also indirect: the secant equation it relies on becomes a poor proxy for the Newton step precisely when the problem is badly conditioned, which is when you wanted curvature in the first place.

So: is there a way to use the actual Hessian without paying for all of it?

Sketching

Here is the idea. Do not compute the whole Hessian. Sample \(m\) of its columns, where \(m \ll d\), say 10% of them. Now you have a \(d \times m\) slice of the matrix.

A \(d \times m\) slice is not a \(d \times d\) matrix, but the Nyström method lets you reconstruct an approximation of the whole thing from it. The construction is old. It comes from numerical integration, and it is the same machinery behind low-rank kernel approximation. The cost comes out as

\[O(ndm + dm^2)\]

instead of \(O(nd^2 + d^3)\). With \(m = 0.1d\), the \(d^3\) term becomes \(0.01 d^3\), and the \(nd^2\) term becomes \(0.1 nd^2\). Not a constant-factor win: an order-of-magnitude one, and it gets better as \(d\) grows.

In the experiments in our papers, \(m\) between 5% and 20% of \(d\) was enough to get most of the benefit. You can also skip forming the approximation entirely and compute the update \(\delta w\) directly, so neither the full Hessian nor its inverse is ever stored.

The part that nearly kills it

Everything above works on convex problems. Then you try it on a neural network.

On a non-convex objective the Hessian is indefinite: it has negative eigenvalues, because you are sitting near a saddle rather than a bowl. A direction built from an indefinite matrix is not guaranteed to point downhill at all. Your optimizer confidently takes a step that increases the loss.

Worse, the low-rank approximation does not save you. It inherits the problem: approximate an indefinite matrix and you get an indefinite approximation.

The fix is unglamorous and it is the reason the method works: regularize the sketch. Add a multiple of the identity, chosen so the result is positive definite. Now the direction is a descent direction by construction, you get a usable step, and you can prove global convergence.

That is the whole contribution, really. The Nyström part is classical. Making it survive contact with a non-convex loss is the part that took the work.

When not to do this

I want to be straightforward about this, because optimization papers are not always.

  • If \(d\) is small, use Newton. The sketch is machinery for avoiding a cost you are not paying.
  • If your gradients are very noisy (tiny batches, high-variance estimator) curvature estimated from that noise is worse than no curvature. A well-tuned first-order method wins, and it is simpler.
  • If your problem is well conditioned, gradient descent is already close to optimal and the extra complexity earns nothing.
  • You have to choose \(m\). It is a real hyperparameter, the method is sensitive to it, and the right value is problem-dependent. You can study the trade-off, approximation error against \(m\), convergence against \(m\), and we did, but the study informs the choice rather than removing it.

The honest summary: this is a method for large \(d\), ill-conditioned problems where you can afford a full-batch or large-batch gradient. That is a real and recurring setting, and it is not every setting.

Why I still think the direction matters

The ratio between what we spend on gradients and what we learn from them is bad, and it is getting worse as models grow. Every result that makes curvature information cheaper moves that ratio. Not all of them will matter; a sketch that works at \(d = 10^4\) is not automatically a sketch that works at \(d = 10^{10}\), and I would not claim otherwise without running it.

But the arithmetic at the top of this post is not going away, and \(d^3\) is a term worth attacking.

The methods here are from NysReg-Gradient (IJCNN 2026) and the non-convex preprint. MATLAB experiment code is at Nys_Reg; a PyTorch implementation is in preparation.
entry.summary: Second-order optimization is fast and nobody uses it. Here is the arithmetic of why, and what changes if you only look at 10% of the matrix.

entry.title: Smarter Lending: Optimization and Machine Learning in Loan Default Prediction

link.title: Smarter Lending: Optimization and Machine Learning in Loan Default Prediction

entry.content:
Smarter Lending: How Machine Learning and Optimization Are Revolutionizing Credit Scoring

In today’s digital finance ecosystem, the ability to accurately predict whether a borrower will repay a loan is critical for any lending institution. This process, known as credit risk management, has evolved dramatically. Gone are the days of relying solely on historical scorecards and intuition. The new frontier is powered by the synergy of machine learning (ML), which predicts risk with incredible accuracy, and optimization techniques, which help banks make the smartest possible decisions based on those predictions.

This blog post explores how these technologies are transforming credit scoring and default prediction, from the foundational data provided by credit agencies to the sophisticated algorithms that drive modern lending.

The Foundation: Credit Agencies and the Traditional Loan Process

Before diving into advanced analytics, it’s essential to understand the traditional credit infrastructure. Credit Information Companies (CICs) are the data backbone of the lending world.

Agency Country Role & Function
CIC Japan As the only Designated Credit Bureau in Japan, CIC collects and analyzes consumer credit information to support sound lending decisions and prevent excessive consumer debt.
Equifax USA One of the three largest US credit bureaus, Equifax gathers and analyzes consumer credit data, providing credit scores and reports that are fundamental to lending in the US.
CIBIL India Now TransUnion CIBIL, it is India’s largest credit bureau, maintaining credit files on millions of consumers and providing the CIBIL score used by most Indian banks to assess loan risk.

Traditionally, a loan decision followed a structured, manual path:

  1. Application: A borrower submits an application with financial documents.
  2. Data Collection: The lender pulls a credit report from an agency like CIBIL or Equifax.
  3. Financial Scrutiny: An underwriting team manually reviews income, debts, and other financial data.
  4. Risk Assessment: The underwriter makes a judgment call on the borrower’s ability to repay.
  5. Decision: The loan is approved, denied, or approved with conditions.

This process, while established, can be slow and prone to human bias. This is where technology provides a revolutionary upgrade.

The Language of Risk: Key Metrics

To manage credit risk effectively, lenders rely on a set of core metrics. These parameters are the foundation of modern credit risk modeling and are required by global regulatory frameworks like Basel III and IFRS 9.

  • PD (Probability of Default): The likelihood that a borrower will default on their loan within a specific timeframe. ML models excel at predicting this.
  • EAD (Exposure at Default): The total value the lender is exposed to if the borrower defaults (i.e., the outstanding loan amount).
  • LGD (Loss Given Default): The percentage of the exposure the lender will likely lose if a default occurs. It’s the inverse of the recovery rate.

These three components are used to calculate the most critical metric for risk management:

  • EL (Expected Loss): The average financial loss a lender anticipates from a loan. The formula is:

    $EL = PD \times LGD \times EAD$

By accurately predicting PD, machine learning directly improves a bank’s ability to forecast and manage Expected Loss, leading to better profitability and stability.

Machine Learning to the Rescue: What are the Best Models?

Traditional credit models were often too simple to capture the complex, non-linear relationships in a borrower’s financial life. Machine learning overcomes this by identifying subtle patterns in vast datasets that are invisible to the human eye.

While there is no single “best” model, several ML techniques consistently deliver state-of-the-art performance in credit scoring:

Technique Description & Use Case
Logistic Regression A long-standing favorite due to its simplicity and interpretability, making it highly accepted by regulators for PD estimation.
Decision Trees & Random Forests Excellent at handling non-linear relationships and interactions in data. Random Forests, an ensemble method, are robust and less prone to overfitting.
Gradient Boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) Often the top performers for tabular data. These models build decision trees sequentially, with each tree correcting the errors of the last, excelling at handling imbalanced datasets.
Support Vector Machines (SVM) A powerful classification technique effective for high-dimensional data, finding the optimal boundary to separate defaulters from non-defaulters.
Neural Networks Best suited for capturing highly complex patterns in very large datasets, though they are often less interpretable than other models.
AutoML Platforms Tools like H2O.ai or Google AutoML automate the process of feature engineering, model selection, and hyperparameter tuning to find the best-performing model quickly.

Optimization: From Prediction to Profitable Decision-Making

While ML models predict risk, optimization techniques help banks make the best possible decisions based on those predictions. This is about moving from “who is risky?” to “what is the best action to take?”.

Key Applications of Optimization:

  • Threshold Optimization: Setting the ideal credit score cut-off to approve or deny applicants, balancing the risk of defaults against the opportunity cost of rejecting good customers.
  • Portfolio Optimization: Strategically building a loan portfolio that maximizes returns for a given level of risk appetite.
  • Loan Pricing: Personalizing interest rates based on an applicant’s predicted risk (PD), ensuring that prices cover the Expected Loss and generate profit.
  • Hyperparameter Tuning: Using methods like Grid Search or Genetic Algorithms to fine-tune ML models and maximize their predictive accuracy.

A classic optimization problem in lending is to maximize profitability, subject to regulatory and capital constraints:

Maximize: (Revenue from Loans) – (Expected Losses) – (Capital Costs)

Subject to: Credit policy rules and risk thresholds

How Can Optimization Reduce Non-Performing Loans (NPLs)?

NPLs are a major threat to a bank’s financial health. Optimization provides a proactive defense by:

  • Creating Early Warning Systems: Identifying high-risk borrowers early so the bank can take preventative action.
  • Enabling Dynamic Credit Policies: Continuously adjusting lending rules and collateral requirements based on real-time risk data.
  • Optimizing Collections: Prioritizing recovery efforts on accounts with the highest expected return.

The Heart of the Model: Objective and Loss Functions

Every ML model learns by trying to minimize a loss function (or objective function). In credit scoring, a binary classification problem (default vs. non-default), the choice of loss function is critical, especially due to imbalanced data—where defaulters are rare compared to non-defaulters.

  • Standard Function: Binary Cross-Entropy (Log Loss) is a common starting point.
  • Functions for Imbalance: To force the model to pay attention to the rare default cases, more advanced functions are used:
    • Weighted Cross-Entropy: Assigns a higher penalty for misclassifying a defaulter.
    • Focal Loss: Down-weights the loss for easy-to-classify (often non-default) cases, allowing the model to focus on difficult, high-risk applicants.
    • Custom Loss Functions: Tailored functions that directly aim to minimize financial loss by incorporating PD, LGD, and EAD into the training objective.

The Modern Loan Approval Pipeline

Putting it all together, a modern, data-driven loan approval process looks like this:

  1. Data Ingestion: Information is gathered from credit bureaus (CIC, CIBIL), KYC documents, and alternative data sources.
  2. PD Modeling: An ML model (like XGBoost) predicts the Probability of Default.
  3. Risk Parameter Estimation: EAD and LGD are estimated based on loan type and collateral.
  4. Expected Loss (EL) Calculation: The core risk metrics are combined: EL = PD × EAD × LGD.
  5. Optimization Engine: The system evaluates the loan terms (e.g., interest rate, credit limit) against the bank’s risk-return objectives to make a final approve/deny decision.
  6. Explainability Layer: Tools like SHAP are used to explain the model’s decision, ensuring transparency for customers and auditors.

Conclusion: The Future of Lending is Here

The integration of machine learning and optimization is transforming credit risk management from a reactive, manual process into a proactive, automated, and highly accurate science. By leveraging these technologies, financial institutions can:

  • Make Faster and More Accurate Decisions: Reducing loan approval times from days to minutes.
  • Reduce Losses: By identifying high-risk applicants more effectively.
  • Maximize Profitability: By optimizing loan portfolios and pricing risk correctly.
  • Promote Financial Inclusion: By using alternative data to score “thin-file” applicants who are invisible to traditional systems.

Ultimately, this data-driven approach creates a more stable, efficient, and equitable financial ecosystem for both lenders and borrowers.
entry.summary: This blog explores how machine learning and optimization are revolutionizing credit scoring and loan default prediction, leading to smarter, faster, and more profitable lending decisions.

entry.title: Accelerating Large-Scale Optimization for Machine Learning

link.title: Accelerating Large-Scale Optimization for Machine Learning

entry.content:
Accelerating Large-Scale Machine Learning: A Deep Dive into SVRG with Barzilai-Borwein Optimization

Gradient noise is the enemy of efficient learning. When you’re training models on millions of data points, mini-batch or stochastic gradient descent (SGD) offers scalability—but at a cost: high variance in updates that leads to slower convergence.

🧮 Objective Functions

This project addresses two main objective functions in convex optimization:

1. L2-Regularized Logistic Regression:

\[\min_w F(w) = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \log(1 + \exp(-b_i a_i^T w)) + rac{\lambda}{2} \|w\|^2\]

2. L2-Squared Support Vector Machine (SVM):

\[\min_w F(w) = rac{1}{2n} \sum_{i=1}^n (\max(0, 1 - b_i a_i^T w))^2 + rac{\lambda}{2} \|w\|^2\]

and each function can be represent as follows:

\[\min_w F(w) = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(w)\]

Where:

  • $a_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$: Feature vector
  • $b_i \in { \pm 1 }$: Binary label
  • $\lambda$: L2 regularization parameter

In this deep dive, I’ll explore a powerful optimization technique I implemented in MATLAB: Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient with Barzilai-Borwein as Second-order Information (SVRG-2BB). It masterfully blends concepts from second-order methods and variance reduction to significantly accelerate convergence on critical convex problems like logistic regression and SVMs, particularly relevant in large-scale machine learning.

The proposed serach direction:

\[w_{t} = w_{t-1} - \eta\ ( abla f_{i_t}(w_{t-1}) - abla f_{i_t}( ilde{w}) + abla F( ilde{w}) + {( ilde{A} - ilde{A}_{i_t}) (w_{t-1} - ilde{w})})\]

We choose BB-approximation in following way,

\[ ilde{A}^k = rac{(s^k)^ op y^ op}{\|s^k\|^2} \mathrm{I} = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} rac{(s^k)^ op ( abla f_{i}( ilde{w}_k) - abla f_{i}( ilde{w}_{k-1}))}{\|s^k\|^2},\] \[ ilde{A}^{k}_{i_t} = rac{(s^k)^ op ( abla f_{i_t}( ilde{w}_k) - abla f_{i_t}( ilde{w}_{m-1}))}{\|s^k\|^2},\]

Where

\[s^k = ilde{w}_k - ilde{w}_{k-1} ext{ and } y^k = abla F( ilde{w}_k) - abla F( ilde{w}_{k-1})\]

Hence, we get

\[ extbf{E}[ ilde{A}_{i_t}] = ilde{A}.\] \[ ilde{A}_{i_t} \approx abla^2 f_{i_t}( ilde{w}) ext{ and } ilde{A} \approx abla^2 F( ilde{w})\]

🔍 Why Variance Reduction?

In vanilla SGD, the update direction is noisy and fluctuates around the true gradient. This inherent noise can severely impede convergence, especially as datasets grow massive.

SVRG (Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient) mitigates this by introducing a control variate—effectively anchoring noisy stochastic gradients to more accurate full-gradient snapshots, taken periodically. This intelligent anchoring significantly reduces the variance of gradient estimates.

But there’s more to truly unlocking speed.

📈 Adding Barzilai-Borwein: Second-Order Speed for Scalability

While SVRG reduces variance, we can further enhance performance by incorporating curvature information without the computational burden of full Hessian matrices. This is where the Barzilai-Borwein (BB) method comes in—a brilliant step-size heuristic derived from quasi-Newton methods that estimates curvature efficiently.

In SVRG-2BB, we integrate BB into the SVRG direction framework to achieve superior acceleration:

  • We utilize BB-approximated step sizes that adapt dynamically within each epoch, leveraging historical gradient information.
  • We preserve and enhance SVRG’s core variance-reduction structure, creating a synergistic effect.

The result is better, more stable convergence, particularly on challenging, ill-conditioned problems common in real-world large-scale datasets.

🧪 Real-world Example: Gisette Dataset

To demonstrate the practical benefits of SVRG-2BB, I evaluated these methods on the Gisette dataset, a well-known challenging high-dimensional classification task. This dataset serves as an excellent benchmark for understanding how optimization algorithms perform under realistic conditions.

Sample Results

Gisette dataset: #n : 6000 , #d: 5001 and $\lambda = 1e-5$

  • ✅ Optimality Gap vs. Epoch
    A visual representation of how closely the algorithm approaches the true minimum of the objective function as training epochs progress. A faster drop indicates quicker convergence.

  • 🕒 Optimality Gap vs. Time
    This plot highlights the real-world efficiency gains. Faster convergence in terms of CPU time translates directly to more efficient model training and quicker iteration cycles in practice.

  • 🔁 Variance of Gradient vs. Epoch
    This figure demonstrates how the Barzilai-Borwein steps, when integrated with SVRG, effectively reduce the inherent stochastic noise across iterations, leading to more consistent and reliable updates.

💡 Why This Matters for Data Scientists: Bridging Theory and Practice

This approach is not just a theoretical advancement in optimization; it has profound practical applications for data scientists working with large-scale data:

  • Large-scale Logistic Regression: Essential for applications like CTR prediction, sentiment analysis, and medical diagnostics.
  • Linear SVMs: Effective for spam filtering, image recognition (e.g., OCR), and text classification.
  • Any Convex Model: Applicable across a broad spectrum of convex machine learning models where minimizing convergence time is critical.

SVRG-2BB bridges the gap between rigorous theory-driven optimization and the demands of practical, high-performance machine learning workflows, offering a path to build more efficient and scalable solutions.

🛠 Try It Yourself

You can explore and run all experiments from this GitHub repo. It provides a clean MATLAB setup for testing various SVRG variants, including the proposed Barzilai-Borwein approximations, allowing you to reproduce and experiment with these powerful optimization techniques.

📚 Further Reading

Journal of Optimization, Industry, and Management. 2024, 20(2): 525-547
